title: Adaptive sparse sampling for quasiparticle interference imaging
author: Oppliger, Zengin, et al.

steps.title: Generate tip travel paths
steps.instruction: From a square grid of size N = n × n select p × qN random locations (q ∈ (0,1] a small fraction) and, for each subset p, compute a near‑optimal traveling‑salesperson (TSP) path using either a genetic algorithm or a cheapest‑insertion algorithm with the same fixed start and end coordinates for all paths.

substeps.instruction: Limit each path to at most qN = 3000 locations to keep the TSP calculation tractable.
Allow informed‑sampling criteria (e.g., proximity to the border, no‑go areas, high‑LDOS defect sites) when choosing locations.
Record that a genetic‑algorithm TSP for 3000 points takes ≈2.5 h per CPU core (AMD EPYC 7302P); cheapest‑insertion is faster but yields a slightly longer total path length.
Pre‑calculate Σ_{p=100} TSP paths; for a typical experiment use 20–30 of them (≈60 000–90 000 measurement locations).

steps.title: Combine paths with regular topographies
steps.instruction: Begin the experiment by acquiring a regular topography scan centered on fiducial surface features, then interleave TSP path subsets and additional topography scans according to the desired number of consecutive subsets.

substeps.instruction: After each TSP subset, record a regular topography; the scan ends the current ASS iteration.

Create a jittery random‑walk path from the last TSP location to the start of the topography scan, and another jittery path from the last topography location to the start of the next TSP subset to let the piezo settle creep.
Repeat: TSP subset → jittery path → topography → jittery path → next TSP subset, etc.
Correlate successive topography images to obtain the effective displacement caused by thermal drift or residual creep; store this displacement for use in the final QPI coordinate correction.

steps.title: Measure LDOS and preview QPI
steps.instruction: At every location defined by the combined TSP‑topography sequence measure the local density of states (LDOS) and reconstruct the quasiparticle‑interference (QPI) image via sparse‑recovery.

substeps.instruction: Measure LDOS either by conventional bias spectroscopy or by parallel spectroscopy for each selected energy; treat each energy independently.
Record the acquisition timestamp for every spectrum (for possible drift correction).
Feed the growing set of LDOS values into the SPGL1 MATLAB solver (basis‑pursuit denoising) to obtain a QPI image on a 1024 × 1024 grid.
The sparse‑recovery computation for one energy slice takes only a few minutes, enabling a rapid preview of QPI quality after each iteration.

Set STM acquisition parameters: bias Vb = ‑250 mV, drive amplitude Vdrv = 400 mV, drive frequency fdrv = 1600 Hz, tunnelling current It = 1.5 nA, dwell time tspc = 20 ms, temperature T = 4.3 K, grid size 1024 × 1024.

steps.title: Correct tip instabilities
steps.instruction: Apply a global background correction to each TSP segment to remove tip‑change artefacts while preserving spatial LDOS modulations.

substeps.instruction: For each segment s compute mean m_s = Σ_k ρ_Sk ρ_Tk / qN and standard deviation σ_s = Σ_k (ρ_Sk ρ_Tk ‑ m_s)^2 / qN over all bias voltages and locations k.
Choose a reference segment (preferably the first, tip‑stable segment) with mean m_ref and σ_ref.
For every other segment replace ρ_S ρ_T by ρ_S ρ_T' = (ρ_S ρ_T ‑ m_s)·σ_ref/σ_s + m_ref.
If a tip change is detected (e.g., by an edge detector), split the affected segment into sub‑segments and treat the pre‑change part as reference for the remainder.

steps.title: Correct linear drift
steps.instruction: Use the interleaved topography images and timestamps to compensate for linear sample drift across the whole measurement.

substeps.instruction: Determine the global displacement vector v = (v_x, v_y) from image registration between successive reference topographies.
Compute drift speed dv/dt = v / Δt where Δt is the total elapsed time between the two topographies.
For each LDOS location k adjust its coordinates: r_k' = r_k + (dv/dt)·(t_k ‑ t_{k‑1}).
Apply the corrected coordinates before the final sparse‑recovery of the QPI image.

description: In order to validate the functioning for an actual measurement, we choose the well-known model system Au(111), which is characterized by a Shockley surface state and a (22×3) herringbone reconstruction [15]. In our previous work [2], we have measured the dispersion relation of the nearly free electron gas using all combinations of conventional spectroscopy, parallel spectroscopy and sparse sampling for QPI imaging to ensure that our spectroscopies and mapping modes reproduce the Au(111) reference signatures. However, in those measurements we had measured all LDOS values in a single sweep, that is, not adaptively. We proceed here to reproduce these characteristic Au(111) signatures using the adaptive sparse sampling implementation. For the present ASS demonstration, one iteration consists of 5 random walk segments with 3’000 measurement locations each followed by one reference topography. The first iteration is started with an additional topography. Since a reference topography requires about 20 minutes, it can also be interpreted as an interruption/break of the sparse sampling mapping scheme. The panels (a)-(c) in Fig. 2 show the evolution of the QPI reconstruction with an ever-growing number of adaptively sampled LDOS values that are added to the reconstruction with the applied background correction mentioned previously in the post-processing section. From the dispersion plot in panel (a), one clearly notices how more band-structure details emerge with increasing number of measurements. We also see that the states closer to the reciprocal zone center appear at lower sampling than high momentum-transfer states, which is related to the effective level of sparsity at the respective energies in q-space. When the surface state has a higher q-value, it is represented by more wavevector values simply due to the larger circumference [1].
